headline: Singapore runs on punctuality and quiet restraint, so dial back Filipino warmth, cheek-kisses and 'Filipino time' while keeping the food-sharing generosity.

watch_outs.title: Be on time for meetings
watch_outs.from_norm: In the Philippines, business meetings expect on-time arrival but social occasions run on relaxed 'Filipino time'.
watch_outs.to_norm: In Singapore, punctuality is expected in both business and social settings, and arriving late reads as rude.
watch_outs.do: Aim to arrive 5-10 minutes early and message your host the moment you know you'll be late.
watch_outs.avoid: Do not treat a Singapore meeting like a Filipino social gathering and drift in 15 minutes late.

watch_outs.title: Handshake, not cheek kiss
watch_outs.from_norm: Filipinos greet friends and family with a light cheek-to-cheek touch and a soft 'mwah'.
watch_outs.to_norm: Singaporeans default to a light handshake, and many women, especially Malay or Indian, won't extend a hand to a man.
watch_outs.do: Offer a handshake and, if it isn't taken, nod or place your hand over your heart.
watch_outs.avoid: Do not lean in for a cheek kiss or hug someone you've just met.

watch_outs.title: Never touch anyone's head
watch_outs.from_norm: In the Philippines, a light pat on a child's head is a normal affectionate gesture.
watch_outs.to_norm: In Singapore, touching anyone's head, even a child's, is rude across Chinese, Malay and Indian communities.
watch_outs.do: Show warmth with a smile, a wave or a light touch on the shoulder instead.
watch_outs.avoid: Do not pat a colleague's or host's child on the head, however cute.

watch_outs.title: Beckon with a whole hand
watch_outs.from_norm: Filipinos beckon with a palm-down scratching wave, and a curled index finger is already seen as demeaning.
watch_outs.to_norm: In Singapore, curling a single finger to call someone over is read as disrespectful, even hostile.
watch_outs.do: Wave the person over with your whole hand, palm facing down.
watch_outs.avoid: Do not curl your index finger at waiters, staff or colleagues.

watch_outs.title: Right hand at Malay/Indian tables
watch_outs.from_norm: Filipinos eat kamayan-style with either hand and use fork-and-spoon freely, so handedness rarely matters.
watch_outs.to_norm: At Malay or Indian homes in Singapore, use only your right hand to eat, pass dishes and give or receive items.
watch_outs.do: Keep your left hand off the food and dishes when eating with your hands.
watch_outs.avoid: Do not eat or hand over a plate with your left hand at a Malay or Indian household.

watch_outs.title: Shoes off, feet tucked
watch_outs.from_norm: Filipinos usually remove shoes at the door, but stretching your legs out at home is unremarkable.
watch_outs.to_norm: In Singapore homes, shoes come off, and at Malay or Indian gatherings you tuck your feet under you rather than point soles at others.
watch_outs.do: Look for the shoe pile, ask 'should I take my shoes off?', and sit cross-legged on floor seating.
watch_outs.avoid: Do not stretch your legs out with soles facing your host or elders.

watch_outs.title: Tip only beyond the service charge
watch_outs.from_norm: Filipinos leave about 10% in cash with the server when no service charge is on the bill.
watch_outs.to_norm: In Singapore, tipping isn't expected, and many bills already add a '++' service charge.
watch_outs.do: Check the bill for '++' first, and if you tip for excellent service, hand it directly to the staff member.
watch_outs.avoid: Do not leave extra cash on the table out of habit.

watch_outs.title: Decline food gently, not flatly
watch_outs.from_norm: Filipino hosts press food on guests, and you accept a token portion or ask to take some home.
watch_outs.to_norm: Singaporean hosts, especially Chinese, may offer once and take a flat 'no' at face value, so a blunt refusal can seem cold.
watch_outs.do: Say 'I'm so full, but it was delicious, thank you' and expect one more offer.
watch_outs.avoid: Do not refuse with a flat 'no, I don't want any'.

watch_outs.title: Choose gifts with care
watch_outs.from_norm: Filipinos bring a modest wrapped gift like local sweets or fruit to a home or first business meeting.
watch_outs.to_norm: In Singapore, gift rules vary by community: halal food for Malay hosts, red/gold wrapping for Chinese hosts, and clocks, sets of four, leather and alcohol are best avoided.
watch_outs.do: Default to a quality food gift, confirmed halal if your host is Malay.
watch_outs.avoid: Do not bring alcohol, leather or a clock unless you know your host well.

watch_outs.title: Quiet noodles, open-hand pointing
watch_outs.from_norm: Filipinos eat mami and batchoy quietly with a spoon, and pointing at objects with an index finger is ordinary.
watch_outs.to_norm: In Singapore, slurping noodles at a hawker centre is fine, but pointing an index finger at people is not.
watch_outs.do: Slurp freely at hawker centres and gesture with an open palm or a nod toward people.
watch_outs.avoid: Do not point your index finger at a person to single them out.
